section.heading: 3.7. Rates of Change in the Natural and Social Sciences
section.paragraph: We know that if $$y = f(x)$$ , then the derivative $$\mathit{dy} \slash \mathit{dx}$$ can be interpreted as the rate of change of $$y$$ with respect to $$x$$ . In this section we examine some of the applications of this idea to physics, chemistry, biology, economics, and other sciences.
Let’s recall from Section 2.7 the basic idea behind rates of change. If $$x$$ changes from $$x_{1}$$ to $$x_{2}$$ , then the change in $$x$$ is

Its limit as $$\left. \Delta x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ is the derivative $$f^{\prime}(x_{1})$$ , which can therefore be interpreted as the instantaneous rate of change of $$\mathbf{y}$$ with respect to $$\mathbf{x}$$ or the slope of the tangent line at $$P({x_{1},f(x_{1})})$$ . section.paragraph: Whenever the function $$y = f(x)$$ has a specific interpretation in one of the sciences, its derivative will have a specific interpretation as a rate of change. (As we discussed in Section 2.7, the units for $$\mathit{dy} \slash \mathit{dx}$$ are the units for $$y$$ divided by the units for $$x$$ .) We now look at some of these interpretations in the natural and social sciences.
section.heading: Physics
section.paragraph: If $$s = f(t)$$ is the position function of a particle that is moving in a straight line, then $$\Delta s \slash \Delta t$$ represents the average velocity over a time period $$\Delta t$$ , and $$\upsilon = ds \slash dt$$ represents the instantaneous velocity (the rate of change of displacement with respect to time). The instantaneous rate of change of velocity with respect to time is acceleration: $$a(t) = \upsilon^{\prime}(t) = s^{''}(t)$$ . This was discussed in Sections 2.7 and 2.8, but now that we know the differentiation formulas, we are able to more easily solve problems involving the motion of objects.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: The position of a particle is given by the equation
where $$t$$ is measured in seconds and $$s$$ in meters.

list.item: (b) What is the velocity after $$2$$ s? After $$4$$ s?
(c) When is the particle at rest?
(d) When is the particle moving forward (that is, in the positive direction)?
(e) Draw a diagram to represent the motion of the particle.
(f) Find the total distance traveled by the particle during the first five seconds.
(g) Find the acceleration at time $$t$$ and after $$4$$ s.
(h) Graph the position, velocity, and acceleration functions for $$0 \leqslant t \leqslant 5$$ .
(i) When is the particle speeding up? When is it slowing down?

example.paragraph: Solution

list.item: (a) The velocity function is the derivative of the position function: $$\begin{array}{cll} s & = & {f(t) = t^{3} - 6t^{2} + 9t} \\ {\upsilon(t)} & = & {\frac{ds}{\mathit{dt}} = 3t^{2} - 12t + 9} \end{array}$$

(b) The velocity after $$2$$ s means the instantaneous velocity when $$t = 2$$ , that is, $$\upsilon(2) = \left. \frac{\mathit{ds}}{\mathit{dt}} \right|_{t = 2} = 3(2)^{2} - 12(2) + 9 = - 3m \slash s$$ The velocity after $$4$$ s is $$\upsilon(4) = 3{(4)}^{2} - 12(4) + 9 = 9m \slash s$$

(c) The particle is at rest when $$\upsilon(t) = 0$$ , that is, $$3t^{2} - 12t + 9 = 3({t^{2} - 4t + 3}) = 3({t - 1})({t - 3}) = 0$$ and this is true when $$t = 1$$ or $$t = 3$$ . Thus the particle is at rest after $$1$$ s and after $$3$$ s.

(d) The particle moves in the positive direction when $$\upsilon(t) > 0$$ , that is, $$3t^{2} - 12t + 9 = 3({t - 1})({t - 3}) > 0$$ This inequality is true when both factors are positive $$\left( {t > 3} \right)$$ or when both factors are negative $$\left( {t < 1} \right)$$ . Thus the particle moves in the positive direction in the time intervals $$t < 1$$ and $$t > 3$$ . It moves backward (in the negative direction) when $$1 < t < 3$$ .

(e) Using the information from part (d) we make a schematic sketch in Figure 2 of the motion of the particle back and forth along a line (the $$s$$ -axis). Figure 2 Details A horizontal line labeled s has two marked points: the first point on the left is labeled t = 0, s = 0; the second point on the right is labeled t = 1, s = 4. Above the line, an arrow begins at the first marked point, runs horizontally rightward, then turns at another marked point labeled t = 1, s = 4, running horizontally leftward, then turns directly above the initial point. This turning point is labeled t = 3, s = 0. It then runs horizontally rightward.

(f) Because of what we learned in parts (d) and (e), we need to calculate the distances traveled during the time intervals $$\lbrack 0,1\rbrack$$ , $$\lbrack 1,3\rbrack$$ , and $$\lbrack 3,5\rbrack$$ separately. The distance traveled in the first second is $$\left| f(1) - f(0) \middle| = \middle| 4 - 0 \middle| = 4m \right.$$ From $$t = 1$$ to $$t = 3$$ the distance traveled is $$\left| f(3) - f(1) \middle| = \middle| 0 - 4 \middle| = 4m \right.$$ From $$t = 3$$ to $$t = 5$$ the distance traveled is $$\left| f(5) - f(3) \middle| = \middle| 20 - 0 \middle| = 20m \right.$$ The total distance is $$4 + 4 + 20 = 28m$$ .

(g) The acceleration is the derivative of the velocity function: $$\begin{array}{rcl} {a(t)} & = & {\frac{d^{2}s}{dt^{2}} = \frac{d\upsilon}{\mathit{dt}} = 6t - 12} \\ {a(4)} & = & {6(4) - 12 = 12{m \slash s}^{2}} \end{array}$$

(i) The particle speeds up when the velocity is positive and increasing ( $$\upsilon$$ and $$a$$ are both positive) and also when the velocity is negative and decreasing ( $$\upsilon$$ and $$a$$ are both negative). In other words, the particle speeds up when the velocity and acceleration have the same sign. (The particle is pushed in the same direction it is moving.) From Figure 3 we see that this happens when $$1 < t < 2$$ and when $$t > 3$$ . The particle slows down when $$\upsilon$$ and $$a$$ have opposite signs, that is, when $$0 \leqslant t < 1$$ and when $$2 < t < 3$$ . Figure 4 summarizes the motion of the particle. example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: If a rod or piece of wire is homogeneous, then its linear density is uniform and is defined as the mass per unit length $$\left( {\rho = m \slash l} \right)$$ and measured in kilograms per meter. Suppose, however, that the rod is not homogeneous but that its mass measured from its left end to a point $$x$$ is $$m = f(x)$$ , as shown in Figure 5.

image.alt: Details A horizontal rod has tick marks x_1 and x_2, in the order from left to right at irregular intervals. The part of the rod, from its leftmost point until a certain point to the left of the tick mark x_1, is labeled x. The text below the part of length x reads, This part of the rod has mass f(x).

example.paragraph: The mass of the part of the rod that lies between $$x = x_{1}$$ and $$x = x_{2}$$ is given by $$\Delta m = f(x_{2}) - f(x_{1})$$ , so the average density of that part of the rod is
$${average density} = \frac{\Delta m}{\Delta x} = \frac{f(x_{2}) - f(x_{1})}{x_{2} - x_{1}}$$

If we now let $$\left. \Delta x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ (that is, $$\left. x_{2}\rightarrow x_{1} \right.$$ ), we are computing the average density over smaller and smaller intervals. The linear density $$\rho$$ at $$x_{1}$$ is the limit of these average densities as $$\left. \Delta x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ ; that is, the linear density is the rate of change of mass with respect to length. Symbolically,
$$\rho = \lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta m}{\Delta x} = \frac{\mathit{dm}}{\mathit{dx}}$$
Thus the linear density of the rod is the derivative of mass with respect to length.
For instance, if $$m = f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ , where $$x$$ is measured in meters and $$m$$ in kilograms, then the average density of the part of the rod given by $$1 \leqslant x \leqslant 1.2$$ is
$$\frac{\Delta m}{\Delta x} = \frac{f(1.2) - f(1)}{1.2 - 1} = \frac{\sqrt{1.2} - 1}{0.2} \approx 0.48{kg} \slash m$$
while the density right at $$x = 1$$ is
$$\left. \rho = \frac{\mathit{dm}}{\mathit{dx}} \right|_{x = 1}\left. = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \right|_{x = 1} = 0.50{kg} \slash m$$

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: A current exists whenever electric charges move. Figure 6 shows part of a wire and electrons moving through a plane surface, shaded red. If $$\Delta Q$$ is the net charge that passes through this surface during a time period $$\Delta t$$ , then the average current during this time interval is defined as
$${average current} = \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t} = \frac{Q_{2} - Q_{1}}{t_{2} - t_{1}}$$

image.alt: Details An illustration shows a cylindrical wire carrying negatively charged particles from left to right through a circular plane surface. The circular surface is shaded in red.

example.paragraph: If we take the limit of this average current over smaller and smaller time intervals, we get what is called the current $$I$$ at a given time $$t_{1}$$ :
$$I = \lim\limits_{\Delta t\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t} = \frac{dQ}{\mathit{dt}}$$
Thus the current is the rate at which charge flows through a surface. It is measured in units of charge per unit time (often coulombs per second, called amperes).

section.paragraph: Velocity, density, and current are not the only rates of change that are important in physics. Others include power (the rate at which work is done), the rate of heat flow, temperature gradient (the rate of change of temperature with respect to position), and the rate of decay of a radioactive substance in nuclear physics.
section.heading: Chemistry

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: A chemical reaction results in the formation of one or more substances (called products) from one or more starting materials (called reactants). For instance, the “equation”
$$\left. 2H_{2} + O_{2}\rightarrow 2H_{2}O \right.$$
indicates that two molecules of hydrogen and one molecule of oxygen form two molecules of water. Let’s consider the reaction
$$\left. A + B\rightarrow C \right.$$

where $$A$$ and $$B$$ are the reactants and $$C$$ is the product. The concentration of a reactant $$A$$ is the number of moles $$\left( 1{mole} = 6.022 \times 10^{23}{molecules} \right)$$ per liter and is denoted by $$\lbrack A\rbrack$$ . The concentration varies during a reaction, so $$\lbrack A\rbrack$$ , $$\lbrack B\rbrack$$ , and $$\lbrack C\rbrack$$ are all functions of time $$(t)$$ . The average rate of reaction of the product $$C$$ over a time interval $$t_{1} \leqslant t \leqslant t_{2}$$ is
$$\frac{\Delta\lbrack C\rbrack}{\Delta t} = \frac{\lbrack C\rbrack\left( t_{2} \right) - \lbrack C\rbrack\left( t_{1} \right)}{t_{2} - t_{1}}$$

But chemists are interested in the instantaneous rate of reaction because it gives information about the mechanism of the chemical reaction. The instantaneous rate of reaction is obtained by taking the limit of the average rate of reaction as the time interval $$\Delta t$$ approaches $$0$$ :
$${rate of reaction} = \lim\limits_{\Delta t\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta\lbrack C\rbrack}{\Delta t} = \frac{d\lbrack C\rbrack}{\mathit{dt}}$$

Since the concentration of the product increases as the reaction proceeds, the derivative $$d\lbrack C\rbrack \slash dt$$ will be positive, and so the rate of reaction of $$C$$ is positive. The concentrations of the reactants, however, decrease during the reaction, so, to make the rates of reaction of $$A$$ and $$B$$ positive numbers, we put minus signs in front of the derivatives $$d\lbrack A\rbrack \slash dt$$ and $$d\lbrack B\rbrack \slash dt$$ . Since $$\lbrack A\rbrack$$ and $$\lbrack B\rbrack$$ each decrease at the same rate that $$\lbrack C\rbrack$$ increases, we have
$${rate of reaction} = \frac{d\lbrack C\rbrack}{\mathit{dt}} = - \frac{d\lbrack A\rbrack}{\mathit{dt}} = - \frac{d\lbrack B\rbrack}{\mathit{dt}}$$
More generally, it turns out that for a reaction of the form
$$\left. aA + bB\rightarrow cC + dD \right.$$
we have

$$- \frac{1}{a}\frac{d\lbrack A\rbrack}{\mathit{dt}} = - \frac{1}{b}\frac{d\lbrack B\rbrack}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{1}{c}\frac{d\lbrack C\rbrack}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{1}{d}\frac{d\lbrack D\rbrack}{\mathit{dt}}$$

The rate of reaction can be determined from data and graphical methods. In some cases there are explicit formulas for the concentrations as functions of time that enable us to compute the rate of reaction (see Exercise 26).

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: One of the quantities of interest in thermodynamics is compressibility. If a given substance is kept at a constant temperature, then its volume $$V$$ depends on its pressure $$P$$ . We can consider the rate of change of volume with respect to pressure—namely, the derivative $$dV \slash dP$$ . As $$P$$ increases, $$V$$ decreases, so $$dV \slash dP < 0$$ . The compressibility is defined by introducing a minus sign and dividing this derivative by the volume $$V$$ :
$${isothermal compressibility} = \beta = - \frac{1}{V}\frac{dV}{dP}$$
Thus $$\beta$$ measures how fast, per unit volume, the volume of a substance decreases as the pressure on it increases at constant temperature.
For instance, the volume $$V$$ (in cubic meters) of a sample of air at $$25{}_{}^{}$$ was found to be related to the pressure $$V$$ (in kilopascals) by the equation
The rate of change of $$V$$ with respect to $$P$$ when $$P = 50{kPa}$$ is

$$\begin{array}{l} {\left. \frac{dV}{dP} \right|_{P = 50} = \left. {- \frac{5.3}{P^{2}}} \right|_{P = 50}} \\ {\phantom{\left. \frac{dV}{dP} \right|_{P = 50}} = {- \frac{5.3}{2500} = - 0.00212m^{3} \slash {kPa}}} \end{array}$$
The compressibility at that pressure is
$$\left. \beta = - \frac{1}{V}\frac{dV}{dP} \right|_{P = 50} = \frac{0.00212}{\frac{5.3}{50}} = 0.02({m^{3} \slash {kPa}}){\slash m}^{3}$$

section.heading: Biology

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Let $$n = f(t)$$ be the number of individuals in an animal or plant population at time $$t$$ . The change in the population size between the times $$t = t_{1}$$ and $$t = t_{2}$$ is $$\Delta n = f(t_{2}) - f(t_{1})$$ , and so the average rate of growth during the time period $$t_{1} \leqslant t \leqslant t_{2}$$ is
$${average rate of growth} = \frac{\Delta n}{\Delta t} = \frac{f(t_{2}) - f(t_{1})}{t_{2} - t_{1}}$$
The instantaneous rate of growth is obtained from this average rate of growth by letting the time period $$\Delta t$$ approach $$0$$ :
$${growth rate} = \lim\limits_{\Delta t\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta n}{\Delta t} = \frac{dn}{\mathit{dt}}$$

Strictly speaking, this is not quite accurate because the actual graph of a population function $$n = f(t)$$ would be a step function that is discontinuous whenever a birth or death occurs and therefore not differentiable. However, for a large animal or plant population, we can replace the graph by a smooth approximating curve as in Figure 7.

Suppose that by sampling the population at certain intervals it is determined that the population doubles every hour. example.paragraph: In Section 3.4 we showed that
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( b^{ x} \right) = b^{ x}\ln b$$
So the rate of growth of the bacteria population at time $$t$$ is
$$\frac{dn}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{d}{\mathit{dt}}{({n_{0}2^{t}})} = n_{0}2^{t}\ln 2$$
For example, suppose that we start with an initial population of $$n_{0} = 100{bacteria}$$ . Then the rate of growth after $$4$$ hours is
$$\left. \frac{dn}{\mathit{dt}} \right|_{t = 4} = 100 \cdot 2^{4}\ln 2 = 1600\ln 2 \approx 1109$$
This means that, after $$4$$ hours, the bacteria population is growing at a rate of about $$1109$$ bacteria per hour.

example.paragraph: When we consider the flow of blood through a blood vessel, such as a vein or artery, we can model the shape of the blood vessel by a cylindrical tube with radius $$R$$ and length $$l$$ as illustrated in Figure 8.

For more detailed information, see W. Nichols, M. O’Rourke, and C. Vlachopoulos (eds.), McDonald’s Blood Flow in Arteries: Theoretical, Experimental, and Clinical Principles, 6th ed. (Boca Raton, FL, 2011).
The average rate of change of the velocity as we move from $$r = r_{1}$$ outward to $$r = r_{2}$$ is given by
$$\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta r} = \frac{v\left( r_{2} \right) - v\left( r_{1} \right)}{r_{2} - r_{1}}$$
and if we let $$\left. \Delta r\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ , we obtain the velocity gradient, that is, the instantaneous rate of change of velocity with respect to $$r$$ :
$${velocity gradient} = \lim\limits_{\Delta r\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta r} = \frac{dv}{\mathit{dr}}$$
Using Equation 1, we obtain
$$\frac{dv}{\mathit{dr}} = \frac{P}{4\eta l}\left( {0 - 2r} \right) = - \frac{Pr}{2\eta l}$$
For one of the smaller human arteries we can take $$\eta = 0.027$$ , $$R = 0.008{cm}$$ , $$l = 2{cm}$$ , and $$P = 4000{{dynes} \slash {cm}}^{2}$$ , which gives
At $$r = 0.002{cm}$$ the blood is flowing at a speed of
$$\begin{array}{l} {{\upsilon(0.002)} \approx {1.85 \times 10^{4}({64 \times 10^{- 6} - 4 \times 10^{- 6}})}} \\ {\phantom{\upsilon(0.002)} = {1.11{cm} \slash s}} \end{array}$$
and the velocity gradient at that point is
$$\left. \frac{d\upsilon}{\mathit{dr}} \right|_{r = 0.002} = - \frac{4000(0.002)}{2(0.027)2} \approx - 74({{cm} \slash s}) \slash {cm}$$

To get a feeling for what this statement means, let’s change our units from centimeters to micrometers $$(1{cm} = 10,000{\mu m})$$ . Then the radius of the artery is $$80$$ μm. section.heading: Economics

example.heading: Example 8
example.paragraph: Suppose $$C(x)$$ is the total cost that a company incurs in producing $$x$$ units of a certain commodity. The function $$C$$ is called a cost function. If the number of items produced is increased from $$x_{1}$$ to $$x_{2}$$ , then the additional cost is $$\Delta C = C\left( x_{2} \right) - C\left( x_{1} \right)$$ , and the average rate of change of the cost is
$$\frac{\Delta C}{\Delta x} = \frac{C\left( x_{2} \right) - C\left( x_{1} \right)}{x_{2} - x_{1}} = \frac{C\left( {x_{1} + \Delta x} \right) - C\left( x_{1} \right)}{\Delta x}$$

The limit of this quantity as $$\left. \Delta x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ , that is, the instantaneous rate of change of cost with respect to the number of items produced, is called the marginal cost by economists:
$${marginal cost} = \lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta C}{\Delta x} = \frac{dC}{\mathit{dx}}$$

[Since $$x$$ often takes on only integer values, it may not make literal sense to let $$\Delta x$$ approach $$0$$ , but we can always replace $$C(x)$$ by a smooth approximating function as in Example 6.]
Taking $$\Delta x = 1$$ and $$n$$ large (so that $$\Delta x$$ is small compared to $$n$$ ), we have
$$C^{\prime}(n) \approx C\left( {n + 1} \right) - C(n)$$
Thus the marginal cost of producing $$n$$ units is approximately equal to the cost of producing one more unit [the $$(n + 1)$$ st unit].

(The cost of raw materials may be proportional to $$x$$ , but labor costs might depend partly on higher powers of $$x$$ because of overtime costs and inefficiencies involved in large-scale operations.)

section.paragraph: Economists also study marginal demand, marginal revenue, and marginal profit, the derivatives of the demand, revenue, and profit functions. These will be considered in Chapter 4 after we have developed techniques for finding the maximum and minimum values of functions.
section.heading: Other Sciences
section.paragraph: Rates of change occur in all the sciences. A geologist is interested in knowing the rate at which an intruded body of molten rock cools by conduction of heat into surrounding rocks. An engineer wants to know the rate at which water flows out of a reservoir. An urban geographer is interested in the rate of change of the population density in a city as the distance from the city center increases. A meteorologist is concerned with the rate of change of atmospheric pressure with respect to height (see Exercise 3.8.19).

In psychology, those interested in learning theory study the learning curve, which graphs the performance $$P(t)$$ of someone learning a skill as a function of the training time $$t$$ . Of particular interest is the rate at which performance improves as time passes, that is, $$dP \slash dt$$ . Psychologists have also studied the phenomenon of memory and have developed models for the rate of memory retention (see Exercise 42). They also study the difficulty involved in performing certain tasks and the rate at which difficulty increases when a given parameter is changed (see Exercise 43).

In sociology, differential calculus is used in analyzing the spread of rumors (or innovations or fads or fashions). If $$p(t)$$ denotes the proportion of a population that knows a rumor by time $$t$$ , then the derivative $$dp \slash dt$$ represents the rate of spread of the rumor (see Exercise 3.4.90).
section.heading: A Single Idea, Many Interpretations
section.paragraph: Velocity, density, current, power, and temperature gradient in physics; rate of reaction and compressibility in chemistry; rate of growth and blood velocity gradient in biology; marginal cost and marginal profit in economics; rate of heat flow in geology; rate of improvement of performance in psychology; rate of spread of a rumor in sociology—these are all special cases of a single mathematical concept, the derivative.

All of these different applications of the derivative illustrate the fact that part of the power of mathematics lies in its abstractness. A single abstract mathematical concept (such as the derivative) can have different interpretations in each of the sciences. When we develop the properties of the mathematical concept once and for all, we can then turn around and apply these results to all of the sciences. This is much more efficient than developing properties of special concepts in each separate science. The French mathematician Joseph Fourier (1768–1830) put it succinctly: “Mathematics compares the most diverse phenomena and discovers the secret analogies that unite them.”
